Feast of Unleavened Bread
FEEST uv un-LEV-end BRED
noun phrase / Hebrew term
Feast (from Latin festum, festival day, celebration) + unleavened (from Old English: prefix un- + leavened, from Old French levain, leaven, fermented dough, from Latin levamen, something that raises) + bread (Old English brēad, piece, morsel, leavened loaf). The Hebrew is Chag HaMatzot (“feast of the unleavened breads”): the seven-day festival immediately following Passover (Nisan 15–21) during which Israel ate no leavened bread. Luke 22:1 uses “Feast of Unleavened Bread” and “Passover” interchangeably, as the two had become fused in common usage by the New Testament era.

See also: Feast of Unleavened Bread

Biblical Definition

The Feast of Unleavened Bread (Chag HaMatzot) is the seven-day covenant festival commanded by God in Exodus 12:15–20 and Leviticus 23:6–8, beginning on the fifteenth of Nisan the day after Passover and continuing through the twenty-first. During these seven days all leaven was to be utterly removed from Israelite dwellings and all bread eaten was to be the flat, unleavened matzot. The feast memorialized both the Exodus haste (Israel left Egypt so suddenly there was no time for bread to rise, Exod 12:39) and the holiness demanded of the covenant people (leaven as the type of corruption and sin's pervasive spread). The first and seventh days were designated holy convocations (Lev 23:7–8) with no customary work permitted. The entire festival was one of the three pilgrimage feasts at which all Israelite males appeared before the LORD at the central sanctuary (Deut 16:16: “the Feast of Unleavened Bread” heading the list). Leviticus 23:6 gives the timing: “And on the fifteenth day of the same month is the feast of unleavened bread unto the LORD: seven days ye must eat unleavened bread.” Exodus 12:17 grounds it in the Exodus event: “You shall also observe the Feast of Unleavened Bread — for on this very day I brought your hosts out of the land of Egypt.” The apostle Paul's application in 1 Corinthians 5:7–8 transforms the seven-day matzot-festival into a permanent moral category for the church: since Christ our Passover has been sacrificed, the church is to be an unleavened community, purging out the old leaven of malice and celebrating the feast with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

Webster 1828 Definition

The Feast of Unleavened Bread (Chag HaMatzot, Lev 23:6–8) is the seven-day Passover-season festival in which Israel removed all leaven from their homes and ate only unleavened bread — memorializing the Exodus haste and enacting the covenant holiness demanded of the redeemed people of God.

FEAST OF UNLEAVENED BREAD. Hebrew Chag HaMatzot: the seven-day festival (Nisan 15–21) commanded in Exodus 12:15–20; Leviticus 23:6–8; Deuteronomy 16:3–8, immediately following Passover; all leaven to be purged from Israelite homes; only unleavened flat bread (matzot) to be eaten.

2. Dual commemoration: (a) the Exodus haste — Israel fled Egypt before their bread could rise (Exod 12:39), so the unleavened bread memorializes the deliverance itself; (b) the covenant holiness — the leaven-free household is an enacted declaration that the redeemed community has been separated from Egypt's corruption and belongs wholly to the holy God.

3. Prescribed holy convocations: the first day (Nisan 15) and seventh day (Nisan 21) were sacred assemblies with no ordinary work (Lev 23:7–8); the entire seven-day span was an elevated season of covenant self-examination and separation from leaven.

4. Pilgrimage requirement: the Feast of Unleavened Bread headed the list of the three mandatory annual pilgrimages to the central sanctuary (Deut 16:16; Exod 23:15; 34:18); every Israelite male was to appear before the LORD with an offering proportional to his blessing.

5. New Testament fulfillment (1 Cor 5:7–8): since Christ our Passover has been sacrificed, the seven-day matzot-festival becomes the permanent moral posture of the church — purging out the leavened man (church discipline, 1 Cor 5:2–5) and celebrating the feast with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

Key Scripture

Exod 12:17 — "And ye shall observe the feast of unleavened bread; for in this selfsame day have I brought your armies out of the land of Egypt: therefore shall ye observe this day in your generations by an ordinance for ever."

Lev 23:6 — "And on the fifteenth day of the same month is the feast of unleavened bread unto the LORD: seven days ye must eat unleavened bread."

Luke 22:1 — "Now the feast of unleavened bread drew nigh, which is called the Passover."

1 Cor 5:8 — "Therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, neither with the leaven of malice and wickedness; but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth."

Modern Corruption

The Feast of Unleavened Bread has been corrupted by historical-critical reduction to a Canaanite agricultural borrowing and by evangelical neglect of the feast's church-discipline imperative that Paul draws from it in 1 Corinthians 5 — so that churches celebrate the Passover season without ever purging out the leaven of tolerated sin.

expand to see more

Critical source analysis treats Chag HaMatzot as a pre-Mosaic Canaanite spring agricultural festival (festival of barley harvest, celebrated with unleavened bread because the new grain had not yet fermented) that was later historicized by the Exodus narrative and attached to Passover by a post-exilic scribal editor. This framework denies the Mosaic institution and the typological intentionality of the leaven-purge. The Reformed confessional position holds that Exodus 12's legislation is exactly what it claims: the LORD's own command at Sinai, grounded in the specific historical circumstances of the Exodus night and designed from its institution to be a type of the covenant community's holiness before the holy God.

The evangelical church's loss of the feast's church-discipline content is the more immediate practical corruption. First Corinthians 5 is Paul's most explicit statement about church discipline, and it is structured as a Passover-season typological argument: you are unleavened (the Lamb has been slain); therefore purge out the leavened man (exercise discipline); celebrate the feast with unleavened sincerity and truth. Churches that practice no meaningful discipline have abandoned the matzot-logic at the very point Paul most directly applies it. The tolerated leaven — the unrepentant, openly sinning member welcomed to the Lord's Table — is precisely what the Feast of Unleavened Bread was designed to end.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Feast of Unleavened Bread roots in the Exodus night's hasty departure (Exod 12:39), in the Mosaic covenant legislation of Exodus 12–13 and Leviticus 23, and in the New Testament's apostolic extension of the leaven-purge to the church's permanent moral call to be an unleavened holy community.

expand to see more

Exodus 12:15–20; 13:3–10 — the original legislation: seven days of leaven-free bread; severe covenant sanction for leavened eating; the feast named and grounded in the Exodus deliverance

Leviticus 23:6–8 — the feast codified in the covenant calendar: the fifteenth of Nisan as the feast's formal beginning; first and seventh days as holy convocations; no ordinary work

Deuteronomy 16:3–8 — the pilgrimage dimension: the bread of affliction eaten “in haste”; the seven-day feast at the central sanctuary; the morning release and return after seven days

First Corinthians 5:6–8 — the New Testament typological application: Christ's sacrifice as the Passover slaughter; the church as an unleavened community; the leaven-purge as church discipline; the feast-celebration as sincerity and truth

Luke 22:1 — the Passover-Unleavened Bread fusion: by the first century the Feast of Unleavened Bread and Passover were practically synonymous in common usage; Jesus' Last Supper occurs within this combined season and is the fulfillment of both

Usage

"Exodus 12:17 grounds the feast in the historical specificity of the Exodus: “on this very day I brought your hosts out of the land of Egypt.” The feast is not a general religious observance about purity; it is a commemoration of a specific dated redemptive act. This historical groundedness prevents the feast's moral demands (no leaven, holiness) from becoming abstract moralism: they are the response of a specific people to a specific divine deliverance. The church's call to holiness is similarly grounded in the specific, dated, historical sacrifice of the Passover Lamb on the cross."

"The fusion of Passover and Unleavened Bread in New Testament usage (Luke 22:1: “the Feast of Unleavened Bread, which is called the Passover”) shows that by the first century these two festivals were experienced as a continuous eight-day arc from the Passover sacrifice to the end of the unleavened-bread season. The theological logic is sound: the sacrifice (Passover) and the holiness it demands (seven days of no leaven) belong together. You cannot celebrate the sacrifice while tolerating the corruption."

"The two holy convocations of the feast — the first day (Nisan 15) and seventh day (Nisan 21) — bracket the entire seven-day period with sacred assemblies. The church's regular Lord's Day gatherings bookend weeks in the same way: the community gathers to begin each week in the Lord's presence and lives out the week as an unleavened community before gathering again. The seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread is a type of the Christian week."
